profile.name: Phathisi
profile.tagline: Bakwena trouser-pegging dance initiated around 1914 in Molepolole.
profile.insight: Originating between 1914 and 1916 in Molepolole, Phathisi mirrors the bicycle-riding mine workers of Botswana who pegged their trousers to avoid the chain.
profile.profile: Phathisi, also known as Borankana, is a traditional dance of the Bakwena tribe in the Kweneng District of Botswana. Estimated to have started between 1914 and 1916, it historically grew out of men tying down their trouser legs with pegs while bicycle commuting. During performances, men and boys dance while women sing, clap hands, and ululate.
profile.profile_long: Phathisi, also alternatively referred to as Borankana, is a traditional music and dance tradition deeply connected to the culture of Botswana, specifically practiced and performed by the Bakwena tribe residing in the Kweneng District, with its center in Molepolole. Historically, performances of Borankana are estimated to have initiated between the years 1914 and 1916. According to historical accounts, the tradition of Phathisi emerged from a very specific utilitarian necessity: men tying down the lowest part of their trousers using a peg when cycling. During this historical era, men frequently worked in mines and relied on bicycles for transportation. Owning a bicycle was a sign of relative wealth, requiring riders to tightly secure their trouser legs to prevent them from being caught in the bicycle chain or causing the rider to topple over. This practical method of trouser pegging was subsequently adapted into the performance style of Borankana, before eventually shifting from pegged trousers to the use of shorts during performances. Traditionally, Borankana was performed exclusively during tribal activities, serving as a vital cultural expression for the community. The performance structure involves distinct gender roles: men and boys are the ones who do the dancing, while females participate actively by singing, clapping hands, and ululating throughout the performance. Both elderly people and young people of the Bakwena tribe participate in keeping this traditional music and dance alive. The dance form bridges daily working-class life—specifically the bicycle commutes of mine workers—with cultural heritage in the Kweneng District. While specific technical descriptions of footwork, posture, musical instruments, and spatial formations are not detailed in the sources, the historical narrative surrounding Phathisi provides a clear window into how practical innovations in daily dress transformed into enduring cultural performance arts within Botswana.

sections.origins_and_history: Phathisi, also known as Borankana, is a traditional music and dance form of the Bakwena tribe in the Kweneng District of Botswana, specifically practiced in Molepolole. Performances are historically estimated to have initiated between the years 1914 and 1916. According to history, Phathisi originated from a man tying down the lowest part of his trouser using a peg while cycling. In the past, men worked in mines using bicycles; owning a bicycle denoted wealth, and trousers had to be tightly secured to prevent them from getting caught in the bicycle chain or toppling the rider. This practical trouser pegging was subsequently adopted into the performance of Borankana, eventually transitioning from pegged trousers to shorts. Historically, Borankana was performed exclusively during tribal activities.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Traditionally performed by men and boys who do the dancing, while females participate by singing, clapping hands, and ululating. The physical movement incorporates the historic practice of trouser pegging or wearing shorts. Detailed footwork, posture, and spatial formations are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: Borankana is traditionally performed as a music and dance form where females sing, clap hands, and ululate to accompany the male dancers. Specific musical instruments and rhythm patterns are not described in sources.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers historically tied down the lowest part of their trousers using a peg, a style derived from bicycle-riding mine workers. This costume detail later transitioned into using shorts for performances. The setting is rooted in tribal activities within the Kweneng District of Botswana, particularly Molepolole.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Historically, Borankana was performed exclusively during tribal activities. It is strongly connected to the culture of Botswana and is performed by both elderly and young people of the Bakwena tribe.
